clips.title: AI Agents Are New. The Security Fundamentals Are Not
clips.why: A security talk that answers the question of this lesson, what to do first about AI agents: start with an inventory, then permissions and owners.
look: Why the first step is knowing which AI systems you have at all.
Permissions and ownership: every system needs a named person and only the access it uses.
Shadow AI: tools that nobody wrote down, which is what a Slack thread for an answer turns into.
clips.after: Our agents.yaml is that inventory, written before most of the agents exist, so no agent starts as shadow AI.

clips.title: IAM for AI: 4 Steps to Secure and Futureproof Agentic Systems
clips.why: IBM's step from ad hoc access to a foundation: agents as their own identities, each with its own, limited access.
look: What changes when an agent gets its own identity instead of borrowing a person's.
How limited, written-down access makes an agent easy to review and easy to switch off.
Which of these foundations our rows already record: owner, keys, repos, channels.
clips.after: Each row in our inventory is one agent identity with its narrowest access, and the broker and the gateway grant only what the row says.

clips.title: Claude Code — For Teams & Enterprise
clips.why: A short tour of server-managed settings, the road our models file takes to every person's Claude Code.
look: Where an admin puts the settings, and that people cannot override them.
How the settings reach each person's Claude Code. Then think about agents, which never sign in to claude.ai.
Think about which settings you would leave alone, as we leave model and effort alone.
clips.after: People get our 10-models.json this way; the agents' VMs get the same file baked into their image, because they reach Claude through the gateway.

practice.q: Which keys line belongs in the row of a planned routine that runs in a sandbox VM?

options.text: keys: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, kept in the VM's environment
options.why: That puts a real key where any command the agent runs can read it. The gateway holds the Anthropic key.
The broker holds GitHub, Jira and Slack, and the gateway holds Anthropic. The VM gets only passes that die with the run.

options.text: keys: the routine's Anthropic key, encrypted at rest
options.why: Encrypted or not, the VM would need the key to use it, so it would be readable while the run works.

practice.q: Byte reviews every pull request on its own, and no person approves each review. Finish its row.
practice.hint: Unattended means no person approves each run.
practice.why: Security reads this field first: an unattended agent gets the strictest rules, such as no Jira writes beyond its own ticket for routines.

practice.q: Put the work on the first version of the inventory in order.
items: Copy Byte's and Vanil's rows from their real configuration
Write the narrowest row for each planned agent
Turn Security's review rules into tests that run on every pull request to the file
Security reviews and approves the first version
Build the broker scopes and the routines' charters to grant what the rows say
practice.why: Describe what is true today first, then decide the plans in writing, check them with tests and a person, and only then build systems that follow the file.

practice.q: Someone added a repo to Byte's own configuration last week, but nobody touched the inventory. who.ts says no agent can touch that repo. What is the right fix?

options.text: Nothing: the inventory only describes planned agents.
options.why: Live agents are in the file too, and a wrong live row gives Security a wrong answer about access that really exists.

options.text: A pull request that brings Byte's row and its configuration back together, reviewed by Security
options.why: Either the row gains the repo with a reason, or Byte is removed from the repo. Both are reviewed decisions, and a test comparing the two catches the next drift.

options.text: Change who.ts so it also reads Byte's configuration
options.why: That hides the gap instead of closing it. Security would still be reviewing a file that does not match reality.

practice.q: Nova's workspace reaches 92 percent of its monthly limit while three Nova runs are working. With hold_new_runs_above_pct: 90, what happens?

options.text: The three runs finish, and new runs wait in the queue
options.why: The hold acts before a run starts, never on a run in progress, because cutting a run throws its work away.

options.text: The gateway starts answering 429 and the three runs stop
options.why: The gateway never refuses a call over budget; it only counts.

options.text: Each run is stopped at its next turn
options.why: No limit cuts a run in the middle. That is exactly what the hold is designed to avoid.
